design_detail: Review article in the New England Journal of Medicine’s Current Concepts series (17 March 2005; nine pages, 50 references) by two medical toxicologists, one at the University of Massachusetts, Worcester, and both at Children’s Hospital, Boston. There is no methods section: no search, selection criteria or appraisal is described. It covers definition and epidemiology, clinical manifestations, mechanisms, diagnosis (a decision algorithm adapted from Dunkley and colleagues), differential diagnosis, management and prevention; the management section gives treatment doses, which this card does not record.
can_establish: How two medical toxicologists described, in 2005, what serotonin toxicity looks like, which drug classes and drug pairs the literature they chose had linked to it, and which diagnostic rule they preferred; it points to primary sources.
cannot_establish: How often any drug pair causes serotonin toxicity or how severe it is (no rate is given for any pair); whether the diagnostic rule it recommends works outside the one unit that derived it (the accuracy figures come from a single source and are not independently confirmed in the review); what happened in the individual cases behind its drug lists; or that mixes it does not list are safe, since no search was done.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review; no search described). Its epidemiology rests on a US poison-centre surveillance report for 2002, a post-marketing study of one antidepressant and one toxicology unit’s registry of 2,222 overdose admissions (Dunkley and colleagues, reference 2), which is also the source of its list of clinical findings and its diagnostic algorithm.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated: no criteria for choosing the 50 references.
sample.selection_effects: The clinical findings and the diagnostic rule come from one source, a single Australian toxicology unit’s overdose registry; the drug lists rest largely on case reports and series, which report what was noticed and published, mostly in overdose or in hospital, and not what happens across all people who take these drugs.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Drug exposure is described as listed in the cited literature: Table 1 lists drug classes and seven interaction pairs or groups.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the causes. Treatment doses appear in the management section and are not recorded in this library.
exposure.polysubstance: The review lists combinations (phenelzine with meperidine; tranylcypromine with imipramine; phenelzine with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; paroxetine with buspirone; linezolid with citalopram; moclobemide with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; tramadol, venlafaxine and mirtazapine) and says that monoamine oxidase inhibitors are strongly associated with severe cases, especially with meperidine, dextromethorphan, serotonin reuptake inhibitors or MDMA. It gives no count of cases for any pair.

outcomes.instruments: The review’s own description of mild, moderate and severe serotonin syndrome by examination findings and temperature (Figures 1 and 2; Manifestations), and the Hunter decision rules as its preferred diagnostic criteria (Figure 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review says the rules were compared with a gold standard, the assignment of a diagnosis by a medical toxicologist (p. 1114); the source paper says there is no gold standard and calls its approach arbitrary.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed. Severity is described by findings: afebrile with tachycardia and reflex changes in mild cases, a core temperature as high as 40 °C in moderate intoxication and more than 41.1 °C in life-threatening cases (p. 1113, no source given for the temperatures).

analysis.effect_sizes: No new analysis. Figures the review quotes from other sources: serotonin syndrome in approximately 14 to 16 percent of people who overdose on SSRIs (reference 8); 26,733 SSRI exposures with significant toxic effects in 7,349 people and 93 deaths in the 2002 US poison-centre report (these count SSRI toxicity in general, not serotonin syndrome); an incidence of 0.4 case per 1,000 patient-months among people taking nefazodone (reference 10); about 60 percent of people with serotonin syndrome presenting within six hours of starting a medicine, an overdose or a change (reference 28); the Hunter rules compared with Sternbach’s criteria, sensitivity 84 against 75 percent and specificity 97 against 96 percent (references 1 and 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: No methods are given, so which studies were left out cannot be judged. The review does not carry over the Hunter rules’ authors’ own cautions: a reference diagnosis from the same unit, a test set that includes the derivation set, and the need for validation in other settings (Dunkley and colleagues, pp. 640–641); it calls the toxicologist’s diagnosis a gold standard.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative synthesis of the literature to 2004: serotonin toxicity is a spectrum from mild to life-threatening caused by excess serotonin, recognised by examination (clonus, reflexes, tremor, agitation, sweating, rigidity, temperature), linked to many drugs and drug mixes and most severely to monoamine oxidase inhibitors taken with other serotonergic drugs; no rate is given for any mix.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review states that monoamine oxidase inhibitors are strongly associated with severe cases, especially with meperidine, dextromethorphan, serotonin reuptake inhibitors or MDMA (p. 1113); that the death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City resulted from meperidine with phenelzine (p. 1112); that its preferred decision rules are simpler, more sensitive and more specific than the original criteria (p. 1115); and that the toxicologist’s diagnosis is a gold standard (p. 1114). Gaps: (1) strongly associated rests on case reports and reviews, with no counts or denominators; (2) the single death is stated as fact and cited to one 1988 article, and how the cause was established is not discussed; (3) the accuracy figures are one unit’s, from a reference its authors call arbitrary, and are presented without their caveats; (4) the temperatures given for moderate and life-threatening poisoning (40 °C and above 41.1 °C) carry no reference and are higher than the severity thresholds in the source the review adapts its rules from.

timeline.event: Sternbach’s criteria, derived from 38 published cases (cited as reference 1 and described in Dunkley and colleagues, p. 636; not read).
Dunkley and colleagues derive and test the Hunter decision rules in one toxicology unit’s overdose registry; the review’s source for its findings list and its algorithm.
This review restates the rules and the 84 against 75 percent and 97 against 96 percent figures without new data.

replication.where_it_stands: A secondary source: its figures for the diagnostic rules and its list of clinical findings trace to one primary paper (Dunkley and colleagues, 2003), which this library has read; its drug lists trace to case reports and earlier reviews that were not read.

funding.funder: A grant from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (DA-14929, to Dr. Boyer) (p. 1119).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed in the article. The journal publishes disclosure forms separately online; they were not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Medical toxicologists at the University of Massachusetts, Worcester, and Children’s Hospital, Boston (p. 1112). Neither author appears in the 50 references. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review of the case literature for each drug pair with counts and a structured appraisal, an independent prospective validation of the decision rules in emergency departments against a reference diagnosis made blind to the rules, and population-level surveillance that counts the people exposed to each pair, so that rates can be stated.

domains.note: No methods section; no search, criteria or selection process described; the 50 references were chosen by the authors.

Some appraisal of treatment evidence (cyproheptadine’s efficacy is called not rigorously established, and some case reports of other treatments probably involved misdiagnosis), but the diagnostic study the review depends on is not appraised and its reference diagnosis is called a gold standard.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Neither author is cited among the 50 references.

Mechanism statements are hedged (several lines of evidence converge), but the temperature figures and the statement about one patient's death are given as fact with no source or discussion, and recommendations are stated as preferences without a stated evidence base.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against the diagnostic rules and the listed drug mixes
domains.note: The rules are presented without their authors’ caveats or any competing criteria beyond Sternbach’s; the drug lists give no sign of how many reports stand behind each entry.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors’ checklist is used. Without a search method the review cannot show that its drug lists are complete or that the evidence for each entry is of any particular strength. It may be cited for how two toxicologists described the condition and its recognition in 2005, for the drug classes and pairs named, and for pointing to primary sources. It may not be cited for the accuracy of the decision rules beyond the source it takes them from, for the risk of any drug pair, or for the temperature thresholds it gives.

key_findings.finding: The review defines the serotonin syndrome as a potentially life-threatening adverse drug reaction that can follow therapeutic use, intentional self-poisoning or an unplanned interaction between drugs; not an idiosyncratic reaction but a predictable result of excess serotonin stimulation of receptors in the central nervous system and the periphery; producing a spectrum from barely perceptible to lethal.

The review states that the death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City more than 20 years earlier resulted from coadministration of meperidine (pethidine, an opioid) and phenelzine (an MAOI), and calls it the most widely recognized example of this preventable condition. It cites a 1988 article in the same journal (reference 4), whose title refers to the case.
key_findings.note: One case stated as fact; the review does not discuss how the cause of death was established.

key_findings.finding: The serotonin syndrome is often described as a triad of mental-status changes, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular abnormalities, but not all are present in every person; signs range from tremor and diarrhoea in mild cases to delirium, neuromuscular rigidity and hyperthermia in life-threatening cases; mild symptoms are easily overlooked.

Quoted from other sources: in 2002 the US poison-centre surveillance system reported 26,733 exposures to SSRIs that caused significant toxic effects in 7,349 people and resulted in 93 deaths (figures for SSRI toxicity generally, not serotonin syndrome); 0.4 case per 1,000 patient-months in people taking nefazodone; more than 85 percent of physicians unaware of the diagnosis; the syndrome occurs in approximately 14 to 16 percent of people who overdose on SSRIs.

The review lists barriers to diagnosis: protean manifestations (tremor, diarrhoea, hypertension or anxiety may be dismissed or put down to mental state), strict use of Sternbach’s criteria that rules out mild, early or subacute cases, and clinicians’ unawareness; the syndrome has been identified at all ages.
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, 3rd paragraph (continues at the top of p. 1113)

key_findings.finding: Drug classes linked to the syndrome include MAOIs, tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs, opiate analgesics, cough medicines, antibiotics, weight-reduction agents, antiemetics, antimigraine agents, drugs of abuse and herbal products. MAOIs that are irreversible or nonselective or that inhibit monoamine oxidase subtype A are said to be strongly associated with severe cases, especially in combination with meperidine, dextromethorphan, SSRIs or MDMA (references 4, 8, 15, 26 and 27).
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs

key_findings.finding: The same paragraph says a single therapeutic dose of an SSRI has caused the syndrome, that adding drugs that inhibit the liver enzymes CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 to an SSRI regimen has been associated with it, and that serotonergic agents given within five weeks after stopping fluoxetine have produced an interaction, presumably through a long-lasting metabolite (reference 13).
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs
key_findings.note: The five-week window is the basis for the first question in the review’s Figure 4.

key_findings.finding: Mild cases may be afebrile with tachycardia, shivering, sweating, dilated pupils, intermittent tremor or myoclonus and brisk reflexes; moderate cases have tachycardia, hypertension and hyperthermia (a core temperature as high as 40 °C is called common), dilated pupils, hyperactive bowel sounds, sweating, and reflex and clonus changes greater in the legs, with mild agitation; severe cases may have severe hypertension and tachycardia that abruptly deteriorate into shock, agitated delirium and muscular rigidity, with a core temperature of more than 41.1 °C in life-threatening cases. Laboratory abnormalities in severe cases include metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, raised aminotransferases and creatinine, seizures, renal failure and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy, many arising from poorly treated hyperthermia.
key_findings.note: No reference is given for the temperatures; Dunkley and colleagues use above 38 °C in their rule and at or above 38.5 °C for severe toxicity.

key_findings.finding: Table 1 lists drugs associated with the syndrome (among them the MAOIs phenelzine, moclobemide, clorgiline and isocarboxazid; the analgesics meperidine, fentanyl, tramadol and pentazocine; dextromethorphan; and MDMA, LSD and Syrian rue among drugs of abuse) and drug interactions associated with severe serotonin syndrome: phenelzine with meperidine; tranylcypromine with imipramine; phenelzine with SSRIs; paroxetine with buspirone; linezolid with citalopram; moclobemide with SSRIs; tramadol, venlafaxine and mirtazapine.

The review describes its main source as the clinical findings in 2,222 consecutive cases of self-poisoning with serotonergic drugs from a toxicology registry, compared with the gold standard of a medical toxicologist’s diagnosis; findings with a significant association were mainly neuromuscular (hyperreflexia, inducible, ocular and spontaneous clonus, myoclonus, peripheral hypertonicity, shivering), with tachycardia, mydriasis, sweating, bowel sounds and diarrhoea, agitation and delirium; a temperature above 38 °C was not as strongly associated but occurred in severely intoxicated people.
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning To better delineate the signs and symptoms (continues at the top of the right-hand column of p. 1114)

key_findings.finding: The onset is usually rapid, with findings often within minutes of a change in medication or self-poisoning; approximately 60 percent of people present within six hours of starting a medicine, an overdose or a change in dosing (reference 28); mild cases may present subacutely or chronically and severe cases may progress rapidly to death.
key_findings.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning The onset of symptoms is usually rapid (top of the right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: No laboratory test confirms the diagnosis; it is inferred from the history and examination. The history should cover prescription and over-the-counter drugs, illicit substances and supplements, and the evolution of symptoms; the examination should assess reflexes, clonus, muscle rigidity, pupils, mouth dryness, bowel sounds, skin colour and sweating.

The authors prefer the decision rules in Figure 4, described as simpler, more sensitive (84 against 75 percent) and more specific (97 against 96 percent) than the original diagnostic criteria (references 1 and 2), and call clonus (inducible, spontaneous and ocular) the most important finding.
Hyperthermia and hypertonicity occur in life-threatening cases, but muscle rigidity may mask clonus and hyperreflexia and so cloud the diagnosis.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, 2nd paragraph (ends at the foot of the left-hand column of p. 1116)

key_findings.finding: Anticholinergic poisoning, malignant hyperthermia and the neuroleptic malignant syndrome are said to be readily distinguished from the serotonin syndrome on clinical grounds and the medication history: for example, normal reflexes, absent bowel sounds and dry skin in anticholinergic poisoning; slow onset over days with lead-pipe rigidity in the neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
key_findings.locator: Diagnosis, paragraphs beginning The differential diagnosis includes, Malignant hyperthermia is, and The neuroleptic malignant syndrome is (right-hand column)

key_findings.finding: Figure 4, the diagnostic algorithm, begins with whether a serotonergic agent has been administered in the past five weeks; if so, the answer is serotonin syndrome when there is spontaneous clonus; tremor with hyperreflexia; inducible or ocular clonus with agitation or sweating; or muscle rigidity with a temperature above 38 °C and ocular or inducible clonus. It is labelled as criteria adapted from Dunkley and colleagues.
key_findings.note: The five-week condition is added by the review; Dunkley and colleagues’ rules say in the presence of a serotonergic agent.

key_findings.finding: Table 2 sets severe serotonin syndrome against anticholinergic poisoning, the neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia by medication history, time to develop (under 12 hours for the serotonin syndrome), vital signs, pupils, mucosa, skin, bowel sounds, muscle tone, reflexes and mental status.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says the rules were compared with the gold standard of a toxicologist’s diagnosis. The source paper says there is no gold standard for clinically significant serotonin toxicity, that its approach was arbitrary for that reason, and that the diagnosis it used is the standard it chose.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reference diagnosis is given more authority than its authors claim for it, which makes the accuracy figures look firmer than they are.

reporting_issues.issue: The 84 against 75 percent sensitivity and 97 against 96 percent specificity are given without saying that they come from one unit’s records, from a test set that includes the records the rules were derived from, with no intervals and no independent test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take the figures as established accuracy; the source’s authors say the rules need validating in other settings.

reporting_issues.issue: Temperatures are given as a core temperature as high as 40 °C being common in moderate intoxication and more than 41.1 °C in life-threatening cases, with no reference, while the rule the review adopts uses above 38 °C and its source treats at or above 38.5 °C as marking severe toxicity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review’s moderate (40 °C) and life-threatening (above 41.1 °C) temperatures sit 1.5 and 2.6 degrees above its source’s severe threshold of 38.5 °C (editors’ calculation), and the review does not reconcile them.

reporting_issues.issue: The surveillance figures (26,733 exposures, 7,349 people with significant toxic effects, 93 deaths) are for SSRI exposures in general; the paragraph is about the serotonin syndrome and gives no count of serotonin syndrome cases from this report.
reporting_issues.consequence: The numbers are not serotonin-syndrome counts and cannot be used as the number of people who had it or died of it.

reporting_issues.issue: The death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City is stated as having resulted from meperidine with phenelzine, on the strength of one 1988 article, with no discussion of how the cause was established or of other possible contributors.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single case stated as fact is a weak basis for the strength of the MAOI and opioid interaction; the review’s other support for it is a table entry without counts.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1112–1120 (full text: opening paragraph, all sections, Tables 1 and 2, Figures 1 to 4, funding line, reference list); paragraph breaks, Table 1 and the sideways Table 2 were checked against page renders. The management section was read for context only and its doses are not recorded. The cited primary sources were not read except Dunkley and colleagues (2003).
